label: Crushed stone → local haul monopoly → housing + public infrastructure

orientation.note: Deliberately not a phase-transition theme. Aggregates is the opposite bet: a low-growth, physically constrained industry whose edge is that nothing changes. Crushed stone has a low value-to-weight ratio, so freight caps the economic haul radius near 25 miles and every quarry is a local oligopoly. The moat is zoning and permitting, not technology, and it deepens as metros make new urban quarries harder to permit. Orientation is therefore about whether unit pricing keeps compounding through a volume downturn, not about whether a new S-curve is starting.

interference.physics_note: Rock is abundant; the binding constraint is transport economics, not geology. Freight is roughly a third of delivered cost, which is what localises the market and creates the pricing power in the first place. Rail and barge extend the radius for a minority of volume and change the competitive map where they do.
interference.economic_note: Unit economics are the whole thesis: freight-adjusted price per ton compounding faster than cash cost per ton. VMC FY2025 cash gross profit was $11.33/ton against $9.46 in FY2023 (+19.8%) while shipments grew 3% -- price, not volume, carried it.
interference.regulatory_note: Zoning and permitting are the moat and the tail risk at once. New reserves near a growing metro are close to un-permittable, which protects incumbents; the same process can contest a renewal on a specific quarry, and company-average reserve life hides that. Aggregates M&A also draws antitrust divestiture conditions (precedent: VMC/US Concrete).
interference.controlled_failures_note: A weak quarter is usually weather -- rain days are a real, recurring, quarterly artefact and are not thesis evidence in either direction. Volume falling while price rises is NOT automatically strength: pricing power and share loss to a local competitor look identical in consolidated numbers, and only market-level disaggregation separates them.

reinforcement.recursive_note: Weakly recursive, and only on the supply side: every year a metro grows, permitting a new nearby quarry gets harder, so incumbent reserves become more valuable without anyone doing anything. There is no demand-side flywheel -- tons shipped track construction activity and nothing the producer does creates more of it.

expected_value_note: Context only. The counter-cyclical claim is that public infrastructure spending cushions a residential downturn: highway and street construction is +4.5% year over year while private residential is -7.3% and single-family starts are -13.5%. Size the public leg against the residential one before assuming it offsets -- know the end-market mix. Federal surface-transportation reauthorisation is the largest single swing factor on this horizon and has no automated source; authorised money converts to shipped tons on a two-to-four-year lag, so obligations lead outlays lead volume. Never auto-inflate Lawrence IRR from any of this.
